title: Knowledge Representation & Expert Systems
html:
Knowledge representation (KR) is about organising what an agent knows — categories, objects, properties, defaults and rules — so that inference is efficient. Expert systems were AI's first big commercial success, and today's knowledge graphs are their descendants.

Main representation schemes

Semantic networks

A graph: nodes are objects/categories, labelled edges are relations (is-a, part-of, has). Properties are inherited down is-a links. Easy to visualise; weak on negation and quantifiers.

Frames

Record-like structures (Minsky, 1974): a frame for Restaurant has slots (cuisine, price) with default values and procedures (“if-needed”). The ancestor of objects and classes in OOP.

Ontologies

A formal, shared vocabulary of categories and relations for a domain. Upper ontologies define general concepts (events, time, physical objects); OWL/RDF encode them as triples; description logics give decidable reasoning.

Rules / production systems

IF-THEN rules over a working memory of facts, fired by an inference engine (forward or backward chaining). Conflict resolution picks which matching rule fires; the Rete algorithm matches efficiently.

Inheritance with exceptions

This is default (non-monotonic) reasoning: birds fly unless we learn otherwise. Classical logic is monotonic — adding facts never removes conclusions — so defaults need special logics (default logic, circumscription) or the inheritance trick above.

Expert systems

ComponentRole
Knowledge baseDomain rules and facts captured from human experts
Inference engineApplies the rules (forward or backward chaining) to the case at hand
Working memoryFacts about the current case (symptoms, test results)
Explanation facilityAnswers why a question is asked and how a conclusion was reached
Knowledge-acquisition interfaceLets experts and engineers add and edit rules
SystemDomainNote
DENDRAL (1965)Inferring molecular structure from mass spectraFirst expert system
MYCIN (1970s)Diagnosing blood infections, recommending antibioticsHundreds of backward-chaining rules with certainty factors; matched specialists but was never used clinically
XCON / R1 (1980)Configuring DEC VAX computersSaved DEC an estimated $40M a year; grew to thousands of rules
Watch out

Why expert systems faded: the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck (experts can't articulate everything), brittleness outside their narrow rules, no learning, and heavy maintenance as rule bases grew. Machine learning replaced much of this — but rule engines still run business logic, and knowledge graphs (Wikidata, Google Knowledge Graph) ground search and LLM answers (retrieval-augmented generation).

Hard problems in KR

ProblemDescription
Frame problemRepresenting what does not change when an action happens without writing an axiom for every unaffected fact
Qualification problemListing every precondition of an action is impossible (the car starts… unless the battery is dead, the tank empty, a potato in the exhaust…)
Closed-world assumptionDatabases and Prolog treat anything not known to be true as false — convenient, but not valid for open worlds like the web
Common senseVast everyday knowledge (water is wet, people have one mother) that is hard to write down — the target of projects like Cyc
Compare semantic networks and frames.

Both organise knowledge around objects and categories with inheritance. Semantic networks emphasise relations as labelled graph edges; frames bundle an object's properties into slots with defaults and attached procedures. They are largely interchangeable and both map to subsets of first-order logic.

What are the components of an expert system?

A knowledge base of rules, an inference engine (forward/backward chaining), working memory for case facts, an explanation facility, and a knowledge-acquisition interface. The user interface asks questions and presents conclusions.
